questions.prompt: A grammar box says that an apposition is the addition of a phrase to another as an explanation. A school magazine prints this line: Nadia Ferchichi, the head of the evening school, answered every letter she was sent. Which words are the apposition?

options.text: the head of the evening school
Nadia Ferchichi
answered every letter she was sent
Nadia Ferchichi answered every letter she was sent

questions.explanation: Look for the group of words that says what somebody is, and you have it: the head of the evening school explains the person just named, and it is fenced by a comma at each end because it has been added to the sentence rather than built into it. The name is the noun being explained, not the explanation. What she did is the ordinary business of the sentence, and lifting the fenced phrase out is what leaves that business standing on its own — which is the test you use on a doubtful comma, not the thing the question asked for.

questions.prompt: A magazine article calls the people it has interviewed cyber students. Who are they?

options.text: learners who sit their end-of-year examination on a computer, in a hall
learners who take their whole course on a screen instead of in a room
learners whose subject is computing, whatever sort of room they sit in
teachers who put their own lessons on the internet for anyone to read

questions.explanation: The word names a way of studying, never a subject and never a job. A cyber student is a learner whose course reaches him through a screen instead of through a room, and what he is studying is left entirely open by the word: it may be law, biology or Spanish. Somebody reading computing has chosen a subject and still walks into a lecture hall to hear about it. Somebody putting lessons online is standing at the teaching end of the wire, not the learning end. And one paper typed on a machine in June says nothing about the fifty weeks that led to it.

questions.prompt: One learner says that following a course from home saves him the journey to the classroom. Another says that the course itself takes as much of his time as it would have taken in a classroom, if not more. Can both of them be right at once?

options.text: no: a course that needs more time cannot also have saved a journey
yes, but only in the case of a learner whose journey was a short one to begin with
yes: the journey and the course are two entirely different calls on a learner's day
no: the minutes saved on the journey come off the time that the course needs

questions.explanation: Two different calls on a day can shrink and grow quite independently of each other, and that is what makes both remarks true together. The bus was never part of the course; it was the price of reaching it. Remove it and the learner's evening is longer, while the reading, the exercises and the written work stay exactly where they were. Treating the saved minutes as though they had been subtracted from the course is the error the whole page is built to catch, and refusing the pair outright, as though one man's longer evening had to be paid for by the other's heavier week, makes the same mistake from the other side. The length of the journey changes the size of the saving and nothing else: eighty minutes or eight, they were spent getting there.

questions.prompt: A guide to earning a degree at a distance argues that this way of studying offers a flexibility no traditional programme can, since it leaves the learner free to study whenever and wherever he chooses. Which two choices is that claim handing him?

options.text: the hour he studies at, and how many hours he owes
the place he studies in, and the subject that his course will cover
the number of hours he owes, and the date by which he has to finish
the hour at which he studies, and the place he studies in

questions.explanation: Two words carry the whole claim, and each hands over one freedom: when says the hour — dawn, midnight, Sunday afternoon — and where says the place, a kitchen or a town with no college in it. Neither word touches the size of the work. How many hours the course will want, and the day it must all be handed in by, are settled by the course itself and are exactly what this freedom leaves untouched; and the subject was chosen before any of this began, by a learner who wanted to study that and not something else.

questions.prompt: A pupil is told to write his letter in formal English, and the instruction gives one reason for it. Which fact about the man he is writing to settles the question of register?

options.text: that he has never met him and does not know him at all
that he has written a book, which the pupil has not done
that he lives in a country other than the pupil's own one
that he is a good deal older than anybody in the pupil's class

questions.explanation: Register follows the distance between two people, and the instruction names that distance exactly: the man is a stranger. That is the whole reason, and it is why the greeting must give him his title and his surname rather than the first name a friend would use. Fame is not the test, or every unknown reader would be written to as an equal and every author as a superior. Nor is a border: you write to your cousin abroad as your cousin. And age would make the same letter informal the day the pupil caught up with him, which no rule of writing has ever said.
